sections.heading: 📖 Using this app with your paper guide
sections.body: Each stop in the Route tab shows a "Paper guide" badge with the matching number(s) from your printed map (the classic A, 1–61 numbering). They mostly line up, with two differences worth knowing: your paper guide doesn't split the Court of the Lions' side halls (Abencerrajes and Two Sisters both sit under its number 29, 'Harem'), and it doesn't number individual spots inside the Generalife — the whole garden is just one unlabelled area there, so those stops show 'Generalife' instead of a number. The Map tab also has a scan of your actual paper map to compare side by side.

sections.heading: ⚠️ Read this first — 2026 earthquake closures
sections.body: Granada had an earthquake swarm in August 2026. As of mid-September: the Alcazaba (including Torre de la Vela) and the Hall of the Ambassadors / Throne Room inside the Comares Tower are CLOSED until further notice. The Patio del Cuarto Dorado also has a protective covering for unrelated roof restoration, so the Comares Façade may be concealed. Everything else on this route — Nasrid Palaces (~95%), Partal, Paseo de las Torres, and the whole Generalife — was reported open in early-to-mid September. Re-check the night before and again at the gate:
list: Official notices: tickets.alhambra-patronato.es/en
Official site: alhambra-patronato.es/en
Visitor phone line: +34 958 027 971

sections.heading: Tickets & ID
list: Alhambra General ticket — includes Nasrid Palaces, Generalife, Partal, Charles V and the Christian buildings.
Tickets are nominative — carry the passport/ID of every named ticket holder. They check.
Your Nasrid Palaces slot is absolute: admission is only within roughly 30 minutes of the stamped time. Miss it and you lose that part of the visit.
Download or print the ticket QR before you go up — mobile signal on the hill is unreliable.
The Alhambra Museum in the Palace of Charles V is free and doesn't need the general ticket.

sections.heading: Security, bags & rules
list: Bag size limit: 40 × 40 cm. Bigger bags go in free left-luggage at the Access Pavilion — a 15–20 min walk from Puerta de la Justicia, so travel light.
Bags are screened at entry, airport-style.
Inside the palaces you may be asked to wear backpacks on your chest, away from the plasterwork.
No tripods, no selfie sticks, no drones.
Photography is allowed; no flash in some rooms — follow posted signs.
Do not touch walls, plasterwork, columns or plants; do not lean on columns.
Do not drink from the fountains or water channels — that's irrigation water, not drinking water.

sections.heading: Water, toilets & food
list: Toilets: Access Pavilion, near the Palace of Charles V, in the Generalife area, near the Puerta de la Justicia. There are NO toilets inside the one-way Nasrid Palaces circuit — go before you enter.
Bring a refillable bottle each — drinking fountains are distributed across the complex. The single best thing to pack.

Food is very limited: the Kiosko near Puerta del Vino (snacks/drinks), the Parador de Granada on Calle Real (café/restaurant, lovely terrace), and a café at the Access Pavilion. Otherwise eat before you go up or after you come down.

sections.heading: Weather & what to wear — 17 Sept 2026
list: Forecast high ≈ 28°C / 82°F, low ≈ 17°C / 62°F. ~50% chance of a light shower — pack a packable rain layer, don't expect much.
Sunrise ≈ 07:59, sunset ≈ 20:18.
Cool at 08:00, hot by noon in the open gardens — dress in layers you can shed.
Footwear: 3.5 km of uneven marble, cobble, gravel and stairs. Proper walking shoes, not sandals.
Hats, sunglasses, sunscreen — little shade in the Generalife's upper gardens or Plaza de los Aljibes.

sections.heading: Best photo windows
list: 08:30–09:30 — Nasrid Palaces: Court of the Myrtles reflection, Abencerrajes vault lit from the east. The whole reason the 08:30 slot is worth it.
09:45–10:30 — Partal pool reflection.
11:00–12:30 — Generalife; the west mirador view is great all morning.
19:45–20:30 — Mirador de San Nicolás, for the exterior at sunset.

sections.heading: Getting up & down
list: On foot from Plaza Nueva: Cuesta de Gomérez → Puerta de las Granadas → woodland path → Puerta de la Justicia. 25–30 min, steep, and the right way to arrive.
Bus C30/C32/C35 from Plaza Isabel la Católica / Plaza Nueva, stops at Justicia and at the Access Pavilion. ~10 min, every ~10 min from early morning.
Taxi: ~€7–9 from the centre.
Walking down through the woods to Plaza Nueva afterward takes ~15 min and is lovely.

sections.heading: The decorative vocabulary — worth knowing before you go in
list: Muqarnas / mocárabes — 3D "honeycomb" plaster vaulting, purely decorative, no structural load. Dissolves the transition from a square room to a dome.
Ataurique / arabesque — carved stucco vegetal scrollwork, pressed from wooden moulds and hand-finished.
Sebka — the diamond/lozenge net pattern covering upper walls.
Zellij / azulejos — geometric mosaic in cut glazed tile, always on the lower walls (dado level): hard and washable below, soft and carved above.

Epigraphy in three scripts — Naskhi (cursive, most common), Thuluth (formal), Kufic (including "knotted" Kufic). Content: Qur'anic verse, dynastic panegyric, and poetry by court poets Ibn al-Jayyab, Ibn al-Khatib and Ibn Zamrak — often written in the first person, so the building speaks to you.
Everything you see as beige/white stucco was originally brightly polychromed — red, blue, gold. Mentally repaint every wall.
Materials: rammed-earth (tapia) and lime concrete walls; white Macael marble for columns and fountains; pine and cedar ceilings; plaster for the decoration. Cheap materials, staggering labour.

sections.heading: History in one screen
list: 1238 — Muhammad I founds the Nasrid dynasty, begins the Alhambra on an 11th-century Zirid fort.
1302–1309 — Muhammad III builds the Partal, the oldest surviving palace on site.
1333–1354, Yusuf I — the Comares Tower, the Hall of the Ambassadors, the Puerta de la Justicia (1348).
1354–1391, Muhammad V — the apogee: the Court of the Myrtles refurbished, the Comares Façade (c. 1370), and the entire Palace of the Lions (1362–1390).
2 January 1492 — Boabdil surrenders Granada. The flag of Castile is raised over the Torre de la Vela the same day.
1527–1637 — Charles V builds his Renaissance palace, demolishing part of the Comares Palace; left roofless until 1967.
1812 — Napoleonic troops mine the towers on withdrawal; a Spanish soldier, José García, disables the fuses and saves the palaces.
1832 — Washington Irving's Tales of the Alhambra, written while living in the Emperor's Chambers, makes the site world-famous.
1923–1936 — Leopoldo Torres Balbás replaces romantic "stylistic restoration" with scientific archaeology; creates most of the gardens.
1984 — UNESCO World Heritage inscription.
2002–2012 — the great Court of the Lions restoration.
Aug 2026 — earthquake swarm; Alcazaba and Comares throne room close.

sections.heading: Scavenger hunt: find the Nasrid motto
sections.body: وَلَا غَالِبَ إِلَّا ٱللَّٰه — Wa lā ghāliba illā Llāh, "And there is no victor but God." Adopted by Muhammad I in 1238, it's carved, tiled, painted and woven thousands of times across the complex. Once you learn the shape of it — the long descender of the lām-alif in illā, the closed loop of Allāh — you'll start spotting it everywhere within twenty minutes. Look especially in:
list: The tile dado and stucco panels of the Cuarto Dorado
The Comares Façade stucco
Repeatedly around the Court of the Myrtles porticoes
The stucco of the Hall of the Ambassadors (viewed from the Court of the Myrtles this year)
Throughout the Court of the Lions portico stucco, including as calligrams worked into the sebka lattice
The Sala de los Abencerrajes and Sala de Dos Hermanas
The Generalife's north pavilion arches
